questions.question: What is the main purpose of a Merkle root?
options: Commit to a whole dataset with one hash
Encrypt a whole dataset with one key
Compress a whole dataset into fewer bytes
Sign a whole dataset without a private key
questions.explanation: A Merkle root is a compact commitment to all leaves under a specific hashing and tree-shape rule.

questions.question: For a tree with n leaves, how large is a typical inclusion proof (number of sibling hashes)?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each tree level contributes one sibling hash, so the proof grows with the tree height, about log2(n).

questions.question: Why does the lesson hash leaves as SHA256(0x00 || encode(leaf)) and internal nodes as SHA256(0x01 || left || right)?
options: To domain-separate leaf hashes from node hashes so they can't be confused
To make the Merkle root longer than 256 bits automatically
To make SHA-256 collision-free for all inputs
To ensure the tree is balanced without duplicating nodes
questions.explanation: Different prefixes ensure a hash intended as a node can't be interpreted as a leaf (and vice versa) in protocols.

questions.question: In this lesson's construction, what happens when a level has an odd number of nodes?
options: The last node is duplicated and hashed with itself to form a parent
The last node is dropped to keep the level even
A random node is added so the tree becomes balanced
The algorithm switches to a ternary (3-ary) tree for that level
questions.explanation: The duplicate-last rule makes the tree shape deterministic for non-power-of-two leaf counts.

questions.question: What does a verifier do with a Merkle inclusion proof?
options: Start from the leaf hash, combine with siblings up the tree, and compare to the known root
Decrypt the root using the proof and recover the original leaf
Check that each sibling hash is prime to ensure integrity
Ask the tree builder for the full dataset and recompute everything
questions.explanation: Verification is purely recomputation: hashing upward until you get a candidate root and checking it equals the expected root.

questions.question: Why does the order (left vs right) matter when hashing internal nodes?
options: Because NodeHash(left, right) is not commutative, so swapping changes the parent hash
Because SHA-256 only accepts inputs where left < right lexicographically
Because Merkle trees require sorted leaves to be secure
Because duplicating the last node forces the order to be irrelevant
questions.explanation: Parent hashes are computed from an ordered concatenation; swapping siblings produces a different digest and breaks the proof.

questions.question: Attack scenario: if a protocol does not domain-separate leaves and nodes, what type of bug can appear?
options: A structural confusion where an internal node hash can be presented as a leaf value
A guaranteed SHA-256 collision for any two leaves
A way to invert SHA-256 and recover the entire dataset
A proof that verifies for every possible root
questions.explanation: Without domain separation, different tree structures can sometimes be interpreted as the same hashed bytes, enabling proof/structure confusion bugs.

questions.question: What must be fixed and agreed upon for a Merkle root to be meaningful across implementations?
options: Leaf encoding, the hashing rules, and the tree shape convention
Only the hash function name (e.g., 'SHA-256')
Only the leaf index of the item being proven
Only the number of leaves in the dataset
questions.explanation: A root commits to bytes under a specific encoding and a specific tree-building rule; changing either changes the meaning of the root.
